item.title: Deobfuscating Auto-Login Wallets in Oracle 26ai
item.description:
After looking into how Oracle obfuscates credential passwords and database link passwords in version 26ai (see also 1 and 2), I started wondering how auto-login wallets are obfuscated and whether the obfuscation has changed in 26ai as well.

Prior public research on that topic dates back to Oracle 11g (see also 3, 4, and 5), and I couldn’t find any information related to 26ai, so I decided to have a look myself.

According to the Oracle 26ai documentation, an auto-login wallet is protected by an obfuscated random password (see also 6):

item.title: Deobfuscating Oracle Credential Passwords
item.description:
In Oracle, credentials are database objects that store a username and password pair for authentication when executing external procedures (extproc callouts), remote jobs, and external jobs (see also 1). More recent Oracle releases also support using credentials with database links (see also 2 and 3).

Credentials are created with the dbms_credential.create_credential procedure, and the associated passwords are stored in obfuscated form in the data dictionary (see also 4). However, Oracle does not publicly disclose the details of the internal obfuscation mechanism and I could not find any publicly available information about it either, which motivated me to take a closer look.

item.title: UUID Generation In Oracle 26ai
item.description:
Some time ago, several bloggers wrote about the new support for UUIDs in Oracle 23ai/26ai (see the blog posts referenced in 1 and 2). This made me curious about how Oracle generates UUIDs behind the scenes and what exactly happens internally when a UUID is created. So, rather than discussing the pros and cons of UUIDs, this note provides a drill-down into Oracle’s UUID implementation details.

Oracle 23.7 introduced a new uuid() function, which generates 128-bit random UUIDv4 values compliant with RFC 9562. Historically, Oracle has provided the sys_guid() function, but the values it generates are predictable and not truly random.
